rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so we have zero information about the performance landscape. The most critical unknown is whether the basic RNA signal alone is informative for this task, which sets the floor against which all encoder, profile, aggregation, and fusion choices must be judged. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest possible RNA configuration—standard PCA dimensionality reduction, a single profile, no aggregation or fusion. It establishes the baseline RNA performance and confirms the pipeline works end-to-end. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Under a limited budget, the highest-value first measurement is the simplest reference point. Every subsequent RNA-based experiment (scvi, scgpt, multiprofile, multimodal) will be interpreted relative to this floor. Starting with a more complex configuration (e.g., multimodal or scgpt) would conflate multiple design choices and make it impossible to attribute performance gains to any single factor. A simple PCA baseline also carries minimal risk of implementation failure, ensuring the first budget slot yields clean, interpretable data.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: We have a single data point (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc). We know nothing about whether the image modality contributes useful signal, which is the central premise of a multimodal study. 2) What this tests: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) provides a clean single-modality baseline for the image branch, directly answering whether spatial/morphological features are informative for this task. 3) Why best next: This is the highest-uncertainty, highest-leverage question. If image features are uninformative, the entire multimodal block (configs 016–051) is deprioritized and we should invest in RNA encoder or profile-setting improvements. If they are informative, multimodal fusion becomes a promising exploitation direction. Using resnet50 (the same encoder in configs 016–021) and keeping singleprofile ensures a controlled comparison: later, config_016 vs config_010 vs config_001 will cleanly isolate the additive/fusion contribution of combining modalities. Changing only the modality (keeping profile setting identical) avoids confounding multiple design choices at once.

Evidence: RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 0.485 accuracy while image (resnet50, singleprofile) is only 0.208, making RNA the clearly dominant modality. With only two data points, the most critical uncertainty is whether the RNA representation quality can be improved. Question tested: config_004 changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 (linear) to scvi_n200 (learned nonlinear) while keeping singleprofile constant, giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_001. Why this is the best next step: If scvi_n200 meaningfully outperforms PCA, it establishes that learned representations matter and justifies further encoder exploration (scgpt) and multimodal fusion with a stronger RNA backbone. If it does not improve, it tells us the encoder choice is less impactful than profile structure or fusion strategy, redirecting the search efficiently. This isolates one design axis without confounding changes, maximizing information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: RNA-only models dominate (0.48–0.52) while image-only is weak (0.21), and scvi_n200 outperforms pca_n2000 in singleprofile (0.520 vs 0.485). Uncertainty: We have no data on whether multiprofile aggregation improves upon the best singleprofile RNA result, and this is a key design axis before investing in multimodal fusion. Question: Does moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with simple average-pooling aggregation improve validation accuracy over the current best (config_004, scvi_n200 singleprofile, 0.520)? Why this is the best next experiment: It builds directly on our strongest encoder (scvi_n200), changes only the profile/aggregation axis (the minimal coupled change inherent to multiprofile), and uses the simplest aggregation (avgpool) to isolate whether multiple profiles add signal before introducing transformer complexity. A positive result justifies exploring transformer aggregation and multimodal extensions; a negative result tells us singleprofile suffices, redirecting budget toward encoder choice (scgpt) or multimodal fusion rather than aggregation architecture.

Evidence: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) achieved the best result so far (acc=0.650, F1=0.628), a large jump over config_004 (singleprofile, scvi_n200, acc=0.520). This confirms multiprofile + scvi_n200 is the strongest direction. However, we have no information about whether the aggregation method matters—avgpool is a simple baseline. Question: config_006 (same rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, but transformer aggregation) isolates the effect of aggregation while holding all other variables constant. Why best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005, directly testing whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) can further improve on the already-strong multiprofile scvi result, or whether simple avgpool is sufficient. This informs whether future multimodal experiments should invest in transformer aggregation or whether avgpool is adequate, reducing uncertainty about a key architectural choice before committing budget to more complex multimodal configurations.

Evidence: Multiprofile + scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest direction (0.650-0.653 vs ~0.52 singleprofile), and transformer ≈ avgpool (0.3% gap, likely noise). The image modality is very weak (resnet50: 0.21), so multimodal gains are uncertain. Key uncertainty: whether the RNA encoder choice still matters within the multiprofile setting, and whether an alternative encoder (scgpt) can push past 0.65. Question tested: config_009 changes only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scgpt while holding multiprofile + transformer fixed, isolating the encoder effect in the best-performing structural context. Why this is best: it is a single-variable extension of the current best (config_006), directly exploitative of the strongest signal, and simultaneously tells us whether scgpt is competitive or inferior—information that would guide all future encoder choices. If scgpt matches or beats scvi_n200, we gain a new best; if it lags, we confirm scvi_n200 is well-suited and can focus budget on other axes (e.g., multimodal fusion or image encoder quality).

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_006 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer) at 0.653 acc, while image-only (resnet50) is very weak at 0.208 acc. Aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) is nearly irrelevant for RNA (0.650 vs 0.653). The critical open question is whether the image modality contributes any complementary signal when fused with the strong RNA representation, or whether it merely adds noise. This experiment (config_032: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) directly extends config_006 by adding the image branch with the simplest standard fusion (concat), isolating the effect of the image modality while holding all other design choices constant. It is the best use of the next budget slot because it answers the highest-uncertainty architectural question—whether multimodal fusion is worth the added complexity—before committing further experiments to multimodal variants. If it fails to beat 0.653, we gain strong evidence to focus on RNA-only improvements; if it helps, it validates the multimodal direction for subsequent experiments.

Evidence: config_032 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) is the best result so far at 0.688 acc / 0.659 F1, outperforming the RNA-only multiprofile baseline (config_006, 0.653) by ~3.5 points. However, we have only tested concat fusion in the multimodal setting; the weighted fusion alternative is completely unexplored. Question: Does the fusion strategy (concat vs. weighted) materially affect multimodal performance, or is the 3.5-point image gain robust to how modalities are combined? Why this experiment: config_033 changes exactly one variable (fusion: concat → weighted) relative to config_032, making it a clean A/B test that isolates the fusion mechanism. If weighted fusion improves performance, it reveals that modality importance is asymmetric and we should invest in tuning weights; if performance is similar, we can rule out fusion strategy as a bottleneck and redirect budget toward improving the image encoder (e.g., ViT-L) or exploring other axes. Under a limited budget, this single-variable comparison maximizes information per experiment by directly extending our strongest result while resolving a fundamental design uncertainty that affects all future multimodal configurations.

Evidence: The best-performing configuration is config_033 (SCVI_n200 + ResNet50, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) at 0.713 acc / 0.695 F1. Image-only ResNet50 is very weak (0.208), yet adding it to the multimodal pipeline yields a meaningful +0.06 gain over RNA-only (0.653→0.713). Weighted fusion clearly outperforms concat (0.713 vs 0.688), and transformer aggregation is the established choice. Uncertainty: We have only tested one image encoder (ResNet50). It is unknown whether a stronger pretrained encoder (ImageNet ViT-L) would extract more useful visual signal and further improve multimodal performance, or whether the image contribution is inherently limited. This experiment (config_039) changes exactly one variable—ResNet50→ViT-L—while holding the rest of the best configuration (SCVI_n200, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) constant. It directly tests whether image encoder quality is a bottleneck, which is a critical architectural decision. If ViT-L improves performance, it validates investing in stronger visual representations; if not, it indicates the image modality's contribution is saturated and further effort should focus on RNA-side improvements. This single-variable comparison is the most informative next step under a limited budget.

Evidence: config_039 (SCVI_n200 + ViT-L, multi-profile, transformer, weighted) is the current best at 0.725 acc. With ResNet50, weighted fusion clearly outperformed concat (0.713 vs 0.688, config_033 vs config_032). Question: Does the weighted-fusion advantage over concat persist with the stronger ViT-L image encoder, or does the richer ViT-L representation make the fusion method less critical? This experiment isolates a single variable (fusion: concat vs weighted) against the current best, providing a clean A/B comparison. Why best next step: It is the most direct exploitation of the top-performing region while simultaneously testing whether a simpler fusion strategy (concat) would suffice, which has practical implications for model complexity. If concat performs comparably, it simplifies the architecture; if it degrades significantly, it confirms weighted fusion is a necessary component and we can confidently lock in config_039's design. No other untested configuration provides as clean a single-variable comparison to the current best.
